articles.title: Impending harsh winter, lack of residential facilities hamper illegal Afghans’ repatriation
articles.description: KHYBER: Hostile socio-economic conditions, acute shortage of residential facilities and an impending harsh winter in Afghanistan have greatly hampered the repatriation of illegal Afghan nationals to their country via the Torkham border since early September. Official sources in Torkham told Dawn that 150-200 Afghan nationals were now crossing the Torkham border crossing on a daily basis compared to 800-1,000 reported in April, May and June. They said that customs terminal and immigration offices were wearing an almost deserted look after a drastic decline in the numbers of returning Afghan families during the last five to six weeks. Afghan refugees gather at a makeshift camp upon their arrival from Pakistan, near the Afghanistan-Pakistan Torkham border. — AFP/File The sources said that the customs authorities also had eased the 100 per cent manual examination of the personal belongings of the returning Afghans as they had earlier received secret information about illegal export of medicine, rice, motorcycles and some other miscellaneous items stuffed in household items of some returning families. Sources say 150-200 Afghans crossing Torkham daily Officials said that as per the legal border crossing procedure, every vehicle had to undergo electronic scanning before being issued a gate pass by the customs authorities, while additional manual examination was made mandatory after complaints about illegal exports. They said all seized items were confiscated by the customs authorities and the border forces that were later placed on auction to ordinary people or local traders. Some of the returning Afghan families lodged complaints about seizure of their costly personal belongings during those customs examinations, both electronic and manual, according to officials. They said that after receiving a lot of complaints from the customs clearing agents who would manage the clearance of personal belongings of the returning Afghan families, only suspicious vehicles were now manually examined. The illegal exports, too, have declined considerably over the past few weeks. Afghans sit inside a tent after their arrival from Pakistan, in Takhta Pul, Afghanistan. —AFP/File Sources familiar with the repatriation process since late March said that while a large number of the illegal Afghans had either been deported or had returned voluntarily, remaining families currently residing mostly in different cities of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa were wary of the political and economic situation in Afghanistan as the repatriated family members or acquaintances had advised them against coming back to their country in the existing circumstances. They said that the affluent Afghans who had gone back had to an extent settled down in different parts of Afghanistan. Sources said those who had yet to decide about their return were informed by the returned Afghans about facing problems in finding suitable living places, acute lack of employment and business opportunities and the fast approaching winter season, which, in most parts of Afghanistan, had become unbearable until March and April. Sources said that a comparatively lenient policy by the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa government had also ‘encouraged’ a good number of the Afghan families to stay back in the province despite being repeatedly “fleeced” by the police or personnel of other law-enforcement agencies. In this file photo from August 2021, people walk inside a fenced corridor as they enter Pakistan through the border in Chaman. — AFP/File Authorities reported a large influx of the returning Afghans after the Torkham border was reopened only for repatriation of illegal Afghan families on March 31 and then onwards in April, May and June with the immigration, customs, Nadra and intelligence personnel struggling to control and manage the repatriation process, according to officials. They said the departments had to make alternate and additional arrangements at the Hamza Baba Transit Centre in Landi Kotal to cope with the growing number of the returning Afghans, especially in the middle of the year. The officials said the centre, too, was wearing a deserted look as the visitors’ number had declined. They added that a number of the food and drinks kiosks established by locals near the centre had been relocated to other places. Published in Dawn, October 2nd, 2026

articles.title: Two Men Spared From Border Patrol Arrest By Upstate NY Protesters
articles.description: Collective action spared two men in Oswego, New York Wednesday following a multi-hour stand-off with federal immigration agents. For seven hours, two men were trapped on the roof of a house in the central New York city as Border Patrol agents attempted to arrest them. But the agency’s efforts were upended when more than 50 people gathered in front of the house and, seemingly, rescued the men from the agents’ clutches. The Oswego Police Department said their officers responded to the commotion after receiving complaints about a reckless driver in the area. Their investigation led them to the private residence on East Seventh Street, where Border Patrol’s Targeted Enforcement Division was attempting to apprehend multiple individuals on federal judicial warrants, according to a police statement. The specific charges of the warrants have not yet been shared, CNYCentral reported Wednesday. Around 5 p.m., the Oswego Fire Department arrived to provide a ladder for the pair of men to climb down. However, it quickly became clear that the men did not want to utilize the ladder, as they kicked and pushed it away from the rooftop’s edge. The fire department then decided to exit the scene, leaving the ladder behind them. “I want to be clear that our efforts last evening were for safety first and not an effort to apprehend individuals,” said Oswego Fire Chief Paul Conzone. “Once we provided the ladder to safely assist the individuals on the roof, we cleared the scene and only returned to retrieve our ladder once the incident concluded.” Border Patrol decided to cut their losses hours later, after which the remaining crowd decided to confront a group of broadcast journalists, throwing articles of clothing over the journalists’ camera lenses while demanding that they stop recording. When the standoff was over, the two men had disappeared from the rooftop and escaped in waiting cars, according to CNYCentral. “I recognize that incidents involving federal agencies can generate strong emotions,” said Oswego Mayor Robert A. Corradino in a statement Thursday. “Even so, our responsibility as a city is clear: we protect our residents, safeguard our neighborhoods, and maintain order.” “Oswego’s strength has always been its people, and yesterday our community showed that even in challenging moments, safety and civility remain our priority,” Corradino added.

articles.title: GOP Senate chief admits deep-red state is slipping out of reach
articles.description: The Republican senator in charge of keeping the party's Senate majority acknowledged this week that one GOP incumbent is in a tighter race than expected in one of the country's most reliably red states. Sen. Tim Scott (R-SC), who chairs the National Republican Senatorial Committee, told Semafor that Kansas has become "more competitive than I'd like to see it," although he still predicted that Sen. Roger Marshall would beat Democrat Adam Hamilton on Nov. 3. "The fact of the matter is that we're going to win in Kansas," Scott said. "It'll be closer than I want it to be." A Democratic win would break a long losing streak for the party in the state. Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932 and has not backed a Democratic presidential nominee since 1964. A Wedgewood poll released last week showed Hamilton with 50 percent support to Marshall's 48 percent, a margin that suggests a close race. The Cook Political Report recently moved the contest from "likely Republican" to "lean Republican." Democrats see Kansas as one of several red states they can contest this year. They point to Trump's low approval ratings and to voter frustration over rising fuel prices tied to the war in Iran. Picking up the seat would boost the party's chances of retaking the Senate. Marshall has appeared to adjust his tone on immigration enforcement. After federal agents carried out operations in Kansas in September, including at meatpacking plants, the senator called for closer cooperation with local authorities. "When ICE operates in Kansas , it needs to coordinate with our local law enforcement," Marshall wrote on X. He has also faced scrutiny over reports that he sued more than 700 patients over unpaid medical bills during his career as an obstetrician-gynecologist. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer told Semafor he welcomes Trump campaigning in competitive states. "When Trump travels, he hurts people," Schumer said. "When he comes to town, that itself helps us."

articles.title: US sees China invasion of Taiwan unlikely before 2028, but trade and market risks remain
articles.description: For years, 2027 has loomed over the Taiwan story as the point by which China wants its military to be capable of taking the island by force. However, the latest US assessment suggests that doesn't necessarily mean an invasion is just around the corner. The latest report from Reuters today says US officials are increasingly seeing a Chinese invasion of Taiwan before 2028 as being unlikely. And that is despite China president, Xi Jinping, having instructed the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) to have the necessary capabilities in place by 2027 if required. Delays to military readiness amid China’s anti-corruption campaign are reportedly one factor, while Beijing is also watching Taiwan’s 2028 presidential election closely. Now, the 2027 date has always been more about military capability than a substantiated invasion timetable on China's part. While they have never publicly confirmed a 2027 readiness order, they also have not ruled out using force to bring Taiwan under their control. But even so, the latest assessment here does help to take a little heat out of the idea that next year could represent some kind of fixed geopolitical deadline. Having said, I wouldn't read this as meaning the Taiwan risk is suddenly something markets can forget about. The timing of this report is particularly interesting as it follows from the recent Trump-Xi summit in Washington. The US and China extended their trade truce for another 60 days, giving both sides more breathing room. However, many of the bigger disagreements - particularly around technology and geopolitics - remain very much in the background. And Taiwan is where those issues start to overlap rather quickly. The island remains deeply embedded in the global semiconductor and AI supply chain. TSMC alone is continuing to expand its manufacturing footprint in the US, highlighting just how strategically important chip production has become to Washington as well as Beijing. Taking that into consideration, the risk isn't just about military conflict for markets. Any meaningful escalation in tensions could quickly spill over into US-China trade relations. And that could lead to further escalation on issues such as tariffs, semiconductor restrictions and investment controls. For traders, the more immediate risk will then fall on tech and Asian stocks. But if the situation worsens, the reaction will likely spread more broadly through global risk sentiment and traditional safe havens. For now, the latest Reuters report arguably pushes the immediate Taiwan timetable further out. However, the bigger takeaway in my view is that Taiwan will continue to remain one of the major fault lines running underneath US-China relations. It won't be an issue that will go away any time soon. As such, markets probably shouldn't price out the geopolitical risk altogether. This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.
